rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance annual allowable rent increase
rules.requirement:
For rent-controlled units under the San Francisco Rent Ordinance, the annual rent increase may not exceed the annual allowable increase published by the Rent Board.

Rates:
- 1.6% of base rent for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.
- 1.4% for March 1, 2025 through February 28, 2026.
- 1.7% for March 1, 2024 through February 28, 2025.

To calculate the increase, multiply base rent by .016. For example, $2,000.00 x .016 = $32.00, giving a new base rent of $2,032.00.

Some tenancies are exempt from the Ordinance's rent increase limits but remain subject to its eviction rules:
- units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979;
- tenancies eligible for a rent increase under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act;
- some tenancies where the rent is regulated by another government agency.

The Rent Board also publishes rates used in capital improvement petitions:
- imputed interest of 4.1% to 4.8% by amortization period, for petitions filed March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027;
- an uncompensated labor rate of $40.40 from 6/29/26.

Some tenancies where the rent is regulated by another government agency
coverage.summary: Rent-controlled units under the San Francisco Rent Ordinance. Units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979 are exempt from the rent increase limits. So are Costa-Hawkins-eligible tenancies and some tenancies regulated by another agency. These exempt units remain covered by the Ordinance's just-cause rules.
coverage.other_conditions: Precedence context: Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12 exempts housing under a stricter local rent control, so this Ordinance's cap governs covered units. Units exempt from the local cap may fall under the state cap if they meet its own coverage rules.

rules.exemptions: Units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979; tenancies eligible for a rent increase under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act; some tenancies where rent is regulated by another government agency.
rules.effective_date_note: The 1.6% rate applies March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 and is reset each March 1. The rate was announced January 14, 2026. The documents do not give the date the Ordinance's rent limits first took effect. The ordinance itself has no sunset; February 28, 2027 ends only the current rate period.
rules.quoted_span: For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable increase amount effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6%.
rules.review_note: No document gives the section number for the annual allowable increase, so the citation stays at chapter level. The cell candidate's claims of a 5% maximum AGA and banked increases came from a passage not among the provided documents. They are not included and need verification. The construction cutoff and exemptions come from the Rent Board's just-cause overview (D079).
rules.source_notes: Official Rent Board announcement (D080) and current rates report (D083) agree on 1.6%. The coverage cutoff is from the official just-cause overview (D079).

also_supported_by.quoted_span: Some tenancies that are exempt from the rent increase limitations of the Ordinance are still subject to the eviction provisions of the Ordinance
This includes tenancies in newly constructed rental units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just cause eviction and relocation payments (§§ 37.9(a), 37.9A, 37.9C)
rules.key_value: 17 just causes; dominant motive required. Notices served 3/1/2026–2/28/2027: § 37.9C evictions (owner/relative move-in, demolition/permanent removal, temporary capital improvement, substantial rehabilitation) $8,245.00 per tenant, max $24,733.00 per unit, plus $5,497.00 per elderly (60+) or disabled tenant or household with minor child(ren). Ellis Act (§ 37.9A) $11,110.05 per tenant, max $33,330.13 per unit, plus $7,443.90 per elderly (62+) or disabled tenant. Prior period (3/1/2025–2/28/2026): $8,062/$24,184/$5,375 and $10,863.45/$32,590.33/$7,278.67.

coverage.summary: Rental units covered by the Rent Ordinance. This includes units exempt from its rent increase limits: units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, Costa-Hawkins-eligible tenancies, and some tenancies whose rent is regulated by another government agency.
coverage.other_conditions: No construction cutoff applies to the eviction provisions. The documents do not list exemptions from the eviction provisions themselves.

rules.exemptions: Relocation for temporary capital improvement evictions of less than 20 days is governed by Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9, not § 37.9C.
rules.effective_date_note: No document states when the just-cause provisions took effect. The relocation rate archive begins with notices served 8/10/06 (§ 37.9C) and 3/01/06 (Ellis Act). Relocation amounts reset each March 1 and follow the date the eviction notice is served; current amounts cover 3/1/2026–2/28/2027.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction.
rules.review_note:
The overview does not give notice content or procedures for each cause.

Citations:
- § 37.9C is named on the rate pages.
- § 37.9A for Ellis Act relocation is taken from the link label '578 Multilingual Relocation Payments 37.9A'.

Precedence: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(i) defers to local just-cause ordinances adopted on or before Sept. 1, 2019, or to more protective later ones. The documents do not state this Ordinance's adoption date, so supersedes_state_rule is left null. The relocation archive dating to 2006 suggests the Ordinance predates 2019.
rules.source_notes: Official Rent Board overview (D079) and official rate pages (D082 archive, D083 current rates). The four relocation candidates describe §§ 37.9A and 37.9C of the same Rent Ordinance and are folded in here.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: Relocation Payments for Evictions based on Owner/Relative Move-in OR Demolition/Permanent Removal of Unit from Housing Use OR Temporary Capital Improvement Work* OR Substantial Rehabilitation
*The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions for less than 20 days is governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 and not by Rent Ordinance Section 37.9C.

rules.title: San Francisco annual security deposit interest rate
rules.requirement: The San Francisco Rent Board publishes an annual interest rate for tenant security deposits: 4.2% for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 (5.0% for 2025–26; 5.2% for 2024–25).

coverage.summary: The rates page does not state which units or deposits are covered.
coverage.other_conditions: The deposit cap and return rules come from Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5 (state). This local interest rate is complementary to it.

rules.effective_date_note: The 4.2% rate applies March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 and is reset annually. The underlying law's effective date is not stated.
rules.citation: San Francisco security deposit interest requirement (code section not stated in documents)
citation_aliases: Rent Board security deposit interest rate
rules.review_note: The Rent Board page publishes the rate but names no legal authority. One candidate's 'S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37' citation was a placeholder and is not used. The governing ordinance, the duty to pay and when interest is due must be verified against the code text. Deposit caps and return deadlines are not stated.
rules.source_notes: Official Rent Board current rates report (D083).

rules.title: San Francisco ban on algorithmic rent-setting devices (Rent Ordinance § 37.10C)
rules.requirement:
The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco. An algorithmic device is a device, such as a software program, that uses algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend to a landlord what rent to charge for a vacant unit.

A tenant or the City Attorney may bring a civil action. Per a secondary source:
- tenants may seek damages, injunctive relief and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation;
- each month of use for each affected dwelling unit may be a separate violation.
rules.key_value: Ban on sale or use of algorithmic devices analyzing nonpublic competitor rental data; civil action by tenant or City Attorney; effective Oct. 14, 2024; per secondary source, civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation, each unit-month potentially a separate violation

coverage.summary: Residential units in San Francisco; reaches both sellers and users of qualifying algorithmic devices. No building-type exemptions are stated.
coverage.other_conditions: Operates alongside the state Cartwright Act common-pricing-algorithm rule (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729); the documents do not address any preemption.

rules.effective_date_note: The Rent Board says the legislation adding § 37.10C took effect October 14, 2024. The law-firm alert's 'effective October 2024' is consistent. Enactment date not stated.
rules.quoted_span: adding Section 37.10C to the Rent Ordinance went into effect on October 14, 2024. The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.
rules.review_note: The ordinance text is not among the documents. The penalty amount and unit-month rule come only from a secondary law-firm alert citing § 37.10C(b) and (d), so verify them against the code.
rules.source_notes: Official Rent Board news notice (D081). Morgan Lewis alert of Aug. 21, 2026 (DX06, secondary). Per DX06, the ordinance is at issue in Gomez v. Greystar Management Services LLC (N.D. Cal.), filed July/August 2026.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: The law prohibits the sale or use of such algorithmic devices and allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action if they believe an entity is in violation of the law.
Each month of use for each affected dwelling unit may constitute a separate violation, and tenants may seek damages, injunctive relief, and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.
